title: The spring science evidence exchange
subtitle: A short checkpoint in explaining, comparing and improving
objective: Use evidence to explain life cycles and apply selected spring science ideas in a teacher-authored checkpoint.

sow.exactOutcome: Consolidate life cycles; evidence spring science (Entry Level Science / UAS).
sow.alignment: Intentional consolidation, teacher-authored evidence checkpoint; no UAS or qualification completion claim. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Recall life-cycle stages, heart pumping and material testing.
Use values with units to support a claim.
success: Describe a life-cycle sequence and a meaningful comparison.
Use material-test data and state a limit.

vocabulary.meaning: Information used to support or challenge a claim.
An account of how or why something happens.
A similarity or difference using the same feature.
A feature used to judge whether work meets the goal.

equipment: Training sheet, one checkpoint route, pencils; optional calculator.
preparation: Give only shared training page 1 during I do and We do. Keep route pages 2–4 face down until You do.
Do not rehearse the checkpoint’s animal names, numerical values or answers before independent work.
Read or scribe neutrally; record any adult prompts separately.
safety: No animal handling, exercise measurements, heat or electrical practical is needed.
Use private feedback and flexible support; do not infer qualification completion from this lesson.
practicalAlternative: All checkpoint evidence is supplied on the selected paper route. No internet or practical materials are needed.

misconceptions.claim: A correct choice alone always proves understanding.
misconceptions.correction: An explanation or evidence link shows more than a guess.
misconceptions.check: Ask which feature or number supports the choice.

misconceptions.claim: A classroom checkpoint gives an official qualification result.
misconceptions.correction: It samples taught ideas for feedback; qualification requirements need separate verification.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the checkpoint was designed to show.

misconceptions.claim: One material result proves what always happens.
misconceptions.correction: A conclusion should name the tested conditions and relevant limits.
misconceptions.check: Ask which extra test would strengthen the claim.

access.supported: Short choices and sentence frames; same three science areas.
access.standard: Explain three evidence cases with a comparison and numerical support.
access.stretch: Evaluate overclaims and suggest a precise next check.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

sources.title: Monarch Joint Venture: Life cycle
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Named monarch sequence: egg, larva, pupa, adult; not a rule for all insects.

sources.title: Arizona State University: Incomplete metamorphosis
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Egg–nymph–adult is different from complete metamorphosis; dragonfly nymphs are aquatic. The checkpoint supplies the necessary species clues.

sources.title: NHLBI: The heart
sources.note: Heart pumping and blood transport reference, checked September 2026.

sources.title: Royal Society of Chemistry: Separation techniques
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Filtration, evaporation and separation misconceptions. Classroom activities are original and include a complete paper route.

sources.title: US National Park Service: Dragonfly larvae
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Aquatic dragonfly juveniles; insects with this incomplete metamorphosis route do not have a pupa.

sources.title: The Wildlife Trusts: Lovely ladybirds
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Explicit ladybird egg, larva, pupa and adult sequence.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: Today is a short teacher-authored checkpoint.
First practise how to use evidence.
The independent cases stay unseen until later.
slides.notes: Explain that this is feedback on selected taught content, not an official exam or grade predictor. Keep selected route pages face down.

slides.title: Remember the evidence habits
body: R1. Why include units with a number?
R2. What does “in this test” tell a reader?
R3. Can an adult read a question without giving the answer?
slides.notes: Units give meaning; bounded context limits a claim; yes, neutral reading supports access. Do not review the checkpoint’s exact factual answers.

slides.title: I model how to answer, not the checkpoint
body: I read the question before choosing evidence.
I select a matching observation.
I explain the link in one clear sentence.
slides.notes: Think aloud using the training car example only. The purpose is a response routine; the independent lifecycle, body and materials cases are not shown or solved here.

visual.title: A worked example uses evidence
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Read the question; Find a matching
observation; Explain what
it supports. Training example only. Checkpoint cases come later.

elements.text: Training example only. Checkpoint cases come later.

slides.title: I inspect the comparison conditions
body: The training car and ramp height stay the same.
The surface changes.
A fair comparison reduces other explanations.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace the two ramps. This is a schematic, not a scale drawing. Model the control question: What else could change the result? Do not introduce checkpoint values.

visual.title: Training toy-car comparison
visual.description: Two equal-height ramps lead onto surfaces A and B. The same toy car, release point and measuring rule are used. This training example is separate from the independent checkpoint.

elements.text:
Surface A
same car and release

Surface B
same car and release
Same ramp height; change only the surface.

slides.title: I bound the training claim
body: The A values exceed the B values here.
I use a pair of values with centimetres.
I do not promise the same result everywhere.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model: In these constructed trials, the car travelled farther on surface A, for example 60 cm versus 40 cm in trial 1. Repeat conditions matter. Avoid using the independent insulation data.

visual.title: Separate observation from overclaim
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Observed:
the car travelled farther on A; Supported:
in these trials; Not established:
always, everywhere. Training sample data: A 60, 58 cm; B 40, 42 cm.
A claim must stay within the evidence.

elements.text:
Training sample data: A 60, 58 cm; B 40, 42 cm.
A claim must stay within the evidence.

slides.title: Training editor: improve the response
body: W1. On which surface did the car travel farther in both trials?
W2. Give one pair of numbers and units.
W3. Repair “A always wins everywhere”.
slides.notes: Use the toy-car dataset only. A exceeds B in both trials; 60/40 or 58/42 cm. Replace always with in these sample trials and suggest more repeats or conditions.

table.caption: Constructed training data; different from the checkpoint.

slides.title: Choose useful feedback
body: Response: “A is best because I like it.”
Which feedback helps: add a number, or write faster?
Explain your choice.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Add a numerical comparison that answers the question; speed is not the science goal. Allow private written choice.

slides.title: Prepare for independent work
body: Keep the response routine.
Put the training sheet aside.
Wait for your selected checkpoint page.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Hand out or reveal pages 2, 3 or 4 only after the hinge. No answer key or teacher page should be visible.

slides.title: Which is a useful evidence sentence?
body: Use the training example only.
slides.notes: A unsupported preference. B accurate values/context. C universal overclaim. This tests evidence language, not checkpoint science answers.

options.text: A is better because it looks nicer.
options.feedback: Appearance is not evidence about the measured distance.

options.text: In trial 1, the car travelled 60 cm on A and 40 cm on B.
options.feedback: It gives relevant values, units and a clear boundary.

options.text: The car must always travel farther on A in every situation.
options.feedback: Two training trials do not establish every situation.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Open your selected checkpoint route now.
Work independently on all three science cases.
Ask for reading support if needed.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Use the evidence printed on your route.
Show a reason as well as a choice.
Put a question mark beside anything uncertain.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Submit before seeing the worked answers.
Compare one response with the criteria.
Choose one precise improvement.
slides.notes: Collect the independent checkpoint before discussing its answers. Use the separate teacher answers to give private criterion-based feedback. If pupils annotate afterwards, keep the original response visible so the first attempt is distinguishable.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. Which science area is most secure for you?
E2. Write one corrected explanation after feedback.
E3. Name the evidence that supports it.
slides.notes: Exit is reflection after submission, not a second independent score. Accept a corrected lifecycle, body or material explanation with relevant evidence.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Training only: evidence habits
pupilPages.intro: Use during I do and We do. Keep the checkpoint route face down until You do. The numbers below are constructed toy-car data.

cards.title: Same method
cards.text: Same toy car, ramp height, release point and distance rule. Only the surface changes.

cards.title: Claim to improve
cards.text: “The car always travels farther on A in every situation.” Two trials cannot establish every possible condition.

cards.title: Evidence frame
cards.text: In these trials, ____ . For example, ____ cm compared with ____ cm.

cards.title: Access
cards.text: Questions may be read aloud. A scribe records your own explanation, not an adult’s answer.

blocks.prompt: W1. On which surface did the car travel farther in both trials?
W2. Give one pair of values and units.
W3. Improve the claim and suggest one useful next check.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported checkpoint: three science cases
pupilPages.intro: Open only at You do. Work independently. Teacher may read the words.

blocks.text: Case A: a ladybird has egg → larva → pupa → adult stages. A common frog has egg → tadpole → froglet → adult stages.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which animal has a pupa stage?
S2. Give one life-cycle similarity and one difference.
S3. Which job belongs to the heart?

blocks.text: Case B: constructed cooling data. Same bottles, starting at 30 °C, in a 20 °C room. After 10 minutes: no sleeve 24 °C; thick sleeve 28 °C.

blocks.prompt: S4. Which bottle cooled less in this test?
S5. Explain your choice using one temperature. Does the sleeve stop all energy transfer forever?

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard checkpoint: explain the evidence
pupilPages.intro: Open only at You do. These are new cases and constructed data.

blocks.text: Life-cycle cards: ladybird—egg, larva, pupa, adult; dragonfly—egg, aquatic nymph, adult. Both adults can produce a new generation.

blocks.prompt: N1. Give one similarity and one difference between these cycles. Explain the arrow from adult to new eggs.
N2. Explain how digestion and blood transport work together. State the heart’s job.

blocks.text: Constructed sample data: same bottles and fill, same 20 °C room, one trial per sleeve.

blocks.prompt: N3. Which bottle cooled less? Calculate both falls and explain the effect of insulation.
N4. Give one limit and one useful improvement to this test.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch checkpoint: test the claims
pupilPages.intro: Open only at You do. Support each explanation; do not claim more than the cases show.

blocks.text: Life-cycle evidence: ladybird has egg → larva → pupa → adult. Dragonfly has egg → aquatic nymph → adult. Platypus is an egg-laying mammal whose young receive milk.

blocks.prompt: T1. Evaluate “every young insect becomes a pupa” and “all egg-layers are birds”. Use a named counterexample for each.
T2. Repair “The heart digests food and sends whole crumbs to tissues”. Link two systems accurately.

blocks.text: Constructed data: same bottles and fill; 20 °C room; one trial each.

blocks.prompt: T3. Compare temperature falls. Explain why this does not prove fabric stops all energy transfer.
T4. Design one additional comparison to test thickness. Name a control and the measurement.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Feedback and next step
pupilPages.intro: Complete after submitting the independent checkpoint. This page records improvement, not a new independent score.

blocks.prompt: E1. Which area is most secure: life cycles, body systems or materials? Name evidence from your answer.
E2. Write one corrected scientific explanation after feedback.
E3. What observation, number or process supports the correction?
E4. Choose one precise next practice task.
Reflection. Which kind of support helped you show your own science?

answers.label: R1–R3 / training
answers.answer: Units give a number meaning; in this test bounds a claim; neutral reading can support access without supplying a conclusion. W1 A. W2 60 vs 40 or 58 vs 42 cm. W3 in these sample trials, the car travelled farther on A; repeat and test further conditions. Useful feedback asks for evidence, not writing speed.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A preference is not distance evidence. B correct. C overclaims two trials.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 ladybird. S2 both eggs/adults; ladybird has pupa, frog does not. S3 pumps blood. S4 thick sleeve. S5 28 °C remains closer to the 30 °C start than 24 °C; it slowed cooling, not stopped all energy transfer forever.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 both eggs and reproductive adults; ladybird has pupa whereas dragonfly has nymph and no pupa. Adult→eggs represents new offspring, not the same individual becoming an egg. N2 digestion produces small absorbable nutrients which blood transports; heart pumps blood. N3 falls 6 °C and 2 °C; fabric slowed energy transfer out to the cooler room. N4 one trial limits confidence; repeat matched conditions. Other relevant limitations and specific improvements accepted.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 dragonfly nymph becomes adult without pupa; platypus is an egg-laying mammal. T2 digestive organs break some food molecules down; small nutrients are absorbed and carried in blood; heart pumps. T3 6 °C versus 2 °C; sleeved bottle still cools, so transfer continues. T4 same fabric at two measured thicknesses, matching bottles, fill, starting temperature and room; record temperature after a fixed duration and repeat.

answers.label: Criteria and diagnostic response
answers.answer: Record each area as secure, developing or revisit, without an official grade. Life cycles secure: a valid matched comparison and generational meaning; body systems secure: correct pumping and absorption/transport link; materials secure: correct paired values, slows transfer and bounded conclusion. A correct choice without explanation is developing evidence. Re-teach only the area indicated: stage cards, two-system substance route, or warmer-to-cooler arrow.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: Accept a reasoned self-assessment tied to the submitted work. Corrections must be scientifically accurate and labelled as after feedback. A useful next task names a concept, such as distinguishing nymph from pupa or drawing energy direction, rather than simply “do more science”.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
This is original formative assessment of selected Spring content, not an official awarding-body paper or proof of qualification completion.
The training car example develops the evidence-response routine. The checkpoint uses different organisms, body-system questions and cooling values; do not reveal or rehearse these beforehand.
Interactive training uses only page 1. Collect checkpoint work before answer feedback; preserve the first attempt when pupils correct afterwards.

interactive.title: Training editor: evidence before the checkpoint
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
